stories.title: Roots in the Western Ghats
stories.text: I spent my childhood in a remote village in the forests of the Western Ghats, a Badaga tribal settlement, and the outskirts of a small town, where diverse cultures shaped my outlook on life and leadership. My mother transformed our rented homes into a green oasis, cultivating plants that attracted birds and provided fresh produce, helping us save costs. The healthy meals cooked in earthen pots and the resourceful ways we met our needs ingrained sustainability into every aspect of my life. I studied at a $30-a-year school that attracted children of migrant laborers and underserved communities, creating a vibrant melting pot of cultures and languages. Kho-Kho, often called the poor man's sport, became an instrument of unity amidst this diversity — on the field, we learned to communicate across languages, respect each other's strengths, and build unwavering trust despite our different backgrounds. These experiences forged my first leadership lessons.

stories.title: Family financial background

stories.title: Why an ETA (Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition) Fellowship
stories.text: As a founder, I thrive in ambiguity, value creation, stakeholder management, and asymmetric risk-reward environments, but I find it hard to stay grounded in settings without constant evolution. I'm focused on three capabilities: evolving from a founder's mindset of creation to an operator's mindset of systems and lasting value; cultivating an eye for diligence and integration, especially around leveraging AI and automation to modernize traditional businesses without disrupting cash flows; and building the communication maturity required to guide sellers, employees, and investors through transitions. What excites me most is the 'Operate' phase — stepping into a business a founder has already built, rather than starting one, and combining the operational intuition I developed building MetaXP (PeopleGamez) from scratch with more structured underwriting and deal-structuring frameworks.

stories.text: During the pandemic, I transformed OpenTech into an online format (Project Uplift), which was recognized by the UN for cultivating leadership among students. stories.title: The water-pump collapse that started OpenTech
stories.text: In 2016, my 68-year-old grandmother collapsed from exhaustion while returning from the only water pump 8 miles away. Being the only 'techie' in our remote village, I felt responsible and implemented an IoT-enabled irrigation system. My grandfather then pointed out how many villagers faced similar problems and suggested I teach village children to use technology — shifting my perspective from problem-solving to empowering others. Watching those children gain confidence as they built IoT projects inspired me to launch OpenTech: workshops empowering tribal and slum students to tackle local challenges with technology. Colleagues hesitated to volunteer, citing academic pressure; students skipped sessions to support their families on weekends; even my parents questioned my persistence. My 22-member team and I spent every weekend traveling to some of India's remotest regions, convincing hesitant parents to support their children's ambitions beyond generational jobs. Over three years we helped 10,000+ students build projects like waterbody-cleaning robots and cattle trackers. One student went on to represent India at NASA; many became entrepreneurs. During the pandemic, a former participant and I adapted OpenTech online as Project Uplift, which earned United Nations recognition.

stories.title: The board-game-cafe turnaround
stories.text: Despite initial success, our simulations lacked the depth executives expected, leading to bankruptcy. I had to lay off my team and shut down our office. Operating out of a board-game cafe, I took on consulting projects to close knowledge gaps and volunteered pro bono with thought leaders to gain practical insight into leadership and business-alignment challenges. Over time, I evolved our simulations from basic training kits into full business-consultancy tools — the same toolkit we then used to help five ventures across three countries survive.

stories.title: The hygiene campaign that moved 25,000 women
stories.text: I guided a retail company to uncover cultural stigmas affecting its women-focused product line. By empowering their leadership team, we developed a campaign that engaged teachers, priests, and community leaders to address these barriers. The initiative improved hygiene standards for over 25,000 women while also driving significant product growth — showing how purpose-driven strategy can create both social and business impact.

stories.title: Declining Novartis, and earning 40% equity
stories.text: As recounted by mentor Rishi (TreeForest Capital): when Vikas was introduced to the Madiee team, he had already declined multiple offers from organizations like Novartis to join Madiee — an EBITDA-negative venture with existing liabilities — as a co-founder. His passion was contagious enough that he persuaded exceptional talent from top IITs and IIMs to join as interns and freelancers despite limited incentives, eventually helping the venture support a 100+ member team and turn profitable. Per co-founder Senthil: Vikas joined Madiee pro bono in January 2021, adapted the business to pandemic conditions by finding online board games to facilitate for revenue, and led the team through a strong Toycathon performance — after which Senthil offered him a 40% equity co-founder stake despite initial reservations from advisors. When Vikas eventually resigned, his entire team followed him in solidarity, and he worked to help place the rest of his former team in new roles.
